title: The Women at the Beginning of Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The talk emphasizes the importance of embracing an ordinary, humble approach to spiritual growth, rather than trying to emulate a revered teacher or achieve a specific state of mind. This allows for a deeper connection with one's true nature, characterized by openness, receptivity, and compassion. By cultivating this mindset, we can transcend dualistic thinking and limitations, experiencing freedom and joy in the present moment.

sentences.text: *And unsurpassed, penetrating, imperfect [unclear: "imperfect"] dharma is really met with even in a hundred thousand million kalpas.
Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the [unclear: "Tantangata's"] words.*
Good evening, everybody. [unclear: "Paralls of the Zoom dharma teacher"], I guess.
My new little closet zendo is in the opposite corner from the router, so I need to run the cable there.
I haven't done it yet, so I came back over here to Routerville.
First world problem, I guess.
Well, let's continue our exploration of Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind.
This time around I'm appreciating paying a little more attention to the actual story of the book.
How did this book come to be?
Like so many dharma books, it's not like Suzuki Roshi sat down at his typewriter and wrote a book.
It's more like he gave talks, and in this case many of those talks were pretty spontaneous.
His students recorded them, transcribed them, and edited them like crazy to make this book.

The fascinating thing about this particular book is the setting in which most of the talks were given, and the students who did the work, especially the main student who did most of the editing and arranging.
They were not the top priests and the important-looking people.
They were pretty ordinary-looking people, and not all male, too.
The origin of the book was actually in the living room of a suburban Los Altos, California home, where there was a little sitting group called the Los Altos Zen Group.
Suzuki Roshi came down for a time once a week to lead a sitting and give a short talk after zazen.
This was the home of a woman named Marion Derby.
She organized a tape recorder to record the talks and later transcribe them.
I think back then it would have been a reel-to-reel tape recorder doing the recording, and, of course, the typewriter.
Then these transcripts piled up until there were quite a few of them.
She had the idea that maybe these would be useful for something.
Maybe put them in the newsletter, they've had a lovely newsletter for many decades called Windmill, or maybe it could be a book.
Marion Derby gave a stack of transcripts to Richard Baker, who was at the top of the echelon: a charming, energetic, brilliant priest, I think the first person Suzuki Roshi ordained.
But he was too busy.
He didn't have time to try to make a book, so he invited another woman named Trudy Dixon to take the lead as the editor.
In David Chadwick's biography of Suzuki Roshi, *Crooked Cucumber*, he gives us some more background on who Trudy Dixon was and how she came to practice.
So this is the untold story of this amazing book read by so many, many, many people.
Here's what David wrote about her.
*In the spring of 1968, Richard turned the manuscript over to his good friend Trudy Dixon, who, like Richard, had edited some of Suzuki Roshi's lectures for the Windmill newsletter.
Trudy took on the task, even though she had two small children and had recently undergone surgery for breast cancer and was in poor health.

She threw herself completely into it, listening to the original tapes, painstakingly working on the material word by word, thought by thought, organizing it and conferring often with Richard and occasionally with Suzuki directly.*

*Trudy Dixon had been doing graduate studies in philosophy at UC Berkeley, specializing in Heidegger and Wittgenstein, when her husband Mike took her to Sokoji in 1962 to hear Suzuki lecture* [unclear: "and sidebar"]*.*
Sokoji was the Japanese congregation in Japantown, San Francisco, which was actually Suzuki Roshi's real job.
That's why he was brought to America by the Soto Shu church, to lead this congregation.
It was his gig as a pastor.
He had started doing lectures that were open to the public, and so Trudy Dixon and her husband Mike went.
David goes on.
*Mike was a student at the San Francisco Art Institute.
They arrived late and stood in the back of the zendo.
Suzuki embarked on an unusual line of thought that evening.
He compared the practice of Zen with the study of philosophy, expressing one's truth with one's whole body and mind instead of just being curious about the meaning of life.
He said he'd had a good friend in Japan who was a philosopher and that ultimately his intellectual pursuits just couldn't satisfy him and he killed himself.
At exactly that point in the lecture, Suzuki looked directly and intently at Trudy.
She backed up a few steps.
Trudy could not get that experience out of her mind.
So she and Mike continued coming to lectures and soon decided to start practicing with Suzuki and became close disciples.*
It seems to me, reading a little more of the history, that Trudy Dixon's name really deserves to be on the cover of the book, but it isn't.
She is mentioned in the introduction.
Another time, and you can guess on your own too, we'll hear some of Suzuki Roshi's original speech, the direct transcription.
It's a big job to make it more readable without losing the flavor and style that he was speaking in.
So it was a really hard job.
And not just that she edited and cleaned up the transcripts: she figured out themes and sections and how to arrange things, and decided on the pull quotes at the beginning of each short chapter.
So she really created the book.

Of course, there was some support from Richard Baker and Suzuki Roshi himself, but I get the impression, digging into this a little bit, that pretty much they would just say, "Sure, Trudy, looks great.
Oh, maybe this word here," but basically her design stood.
So, getting back to my concerns about valorization of Suzuki Roshi as the great teacher, capital G, capital T.
Just for a minute, I don't want to overdo this.
He was certainly a great teacher.
Somebody looked up for me the word valorize, which I hadn't actually looked up, and told me its root is to validate.
So something that's very valid if you valorize it, but then going a little too far, a little too valid.
There's no question Suzuki Roshi was the perfect teacher for that situation, for those students, for that cultural moment, for that place.
But it was all co-created.
It wasn't just that Suzuki Roshi broadcast from on high.
I used to feel self-conscious about how much time Norman would spend coming up to be with us, you know what I mean?
Why was he always flying up here for this scrappy little group?
Later I realized, well, it was helping him too.
We were helping to co-create his teaching and develop him as a teacher, just as he helped us develop as students.
So it's the same thing happening here, and happening very directly in this book: Suzuki Roshi and Trudy Dixon co-creating it.
Anyway, Richard Baker's introduction in Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind is what's always triggered me.
It's all about the perfect Roshi and special Zen mind, different from our ordinary minds, which I'm sure is true.
But do we need to make such a big deal about it in that way?
Reading it again today or yesterday, I realized the most over-the-top part is not Richard Baker's words.
The most valorific, if that's a word, piece is what Trudy Dixon wrote, and he quotes her.
Then I remembered that Trudy Dixon died of cancer in her early thirties, very soon after finishing the project.
I don't think she actually saw the book in print.
And then I thought, Tim, chill out.
She deserves to speak.
She deserves to say what she felt about her beloved teacher.
So here are Trudy Dixon's words, with no little footnotes by me.
I'll just celebrate her love for Suzuki Roshi for a minute.
Oops, I've got to open it up for that.
There's Trudy Dixon.
*A Roshi is a person who has actualized that perfect freedom, which is the potentiality of all human beings.
He exists freely in the fullness of his whole being.

The flow of his consciousness is not the fixed repetitive patterns of our usual self-centered consciousness, but rather arises spontaneously and naturally from the actual circumstances of the present.*

*The results of this in terms of the quality of his life are extraordinary: buoyancy, vigor, straightforwardness, simplicity, humility, serenity, joyousness, uncanny perspicacity, and unfathomable compassion.
His whole being testifies to what it means to live in the reality of the present.
Without anything said or done, just the impact of meeting a personality so developed can be enough to change one's whole way of life.
But in the end, it is not the extraordinaryness of the teacher which perplexes, intrigues, and deepens the student.
It is the teacher's utter ordinariness.
Because he is just himself, he is a mirror for his students.
When we're with him, we feel our own strengths and shortcomings without any sense of praise or criticism from him.
In his presence, we see our original face, and the extraordinaryness we see is only our own true nature.
When we learn to let our own nature free, the boundaries between master and student disappear in a deep flow of being and joy in the unfolding of Buddha's mind.*
So that's actually pretty beautiful, isn't it?
I don't know why I had such a thing about it.
One last note about Trudy Dixon, also from David Chadwick.
*In Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind, Trudy put her whole being into expressing the essence of Suzuki's teaching.
After she passed the manuscript on to Richard, she concentrated on taking care of herself in her home in Mill Valley and dealing with her approaching death.
She remained cheerful on the outside, but her mind was possessed with fear, which she revealed to her analyst.

After an operation filled her lungs with liquid and she couldn't breathe, she struggled for breath with all the energy she could find, until she went beyond thoughts, words, and fear into what she later called breath struggle samadhi.*
*After she had undergone five days of difficult recovery, Mike brought Suzuki and Okasan, his wife, to visit her.
She said the sight of them was like seeing the sunrise for the first time.
Then she went to Tassajara and fasted.
And there she had a powerful, joyous experience that included life and death, health and illness, fear and courage.
She said she finally stopped fighting and was accommodating the enemy, as Suzuki described it.
On the verge of death, Trudy had been reborn.
Her analyst said that at her next visit, she seemed like a new person, a fearless and radiant woman.
To her husband, caretakers, and friends, she became an inspiration.*
*Myself, my body, she wrote, is dissolved in phenomena like a sky's rainbow caught in a child's soap bubble.*
*Myself, my body, is dissolved in phenomena like a sky's rainbow caught in a child's soap bubble.*
Thank you, Trudy Dixon, [unclear: "what a great body you saw found"].
These folks are all pretty young.
She's in her early thirties, Richard Baker maybe forty, most of the students in their late twenties and thirties.
Something was happening.
So Trudy and company, of course, as you probably know, start the book with Suzuki Roshi's famous teaching on beginner's mind.
I'm sure you've read this before, but it's really worth hearing again.
Here's a chunk of the chapter, a page and a half.
This is Suzuki Roshi, as channeled by Trudy Dixon.
*In Japan, we have the phrase shoshin, which means beginner's mind.
The goal of practice is always to keep our beginner's mind.
Suppose you recite the Heart Sutra only once.
It might be a very good recitation.
But what would happen if you recited it twice, three times, four times, or more?
You might easily lose your original attitude towards it.
The same thing will happen in your other practices.

For a while, you'll keep your beginner's mind, but if you continue to practice one, two, three years or more, although you may improve some, you're liable to lose the limitless meaning of original mind.*
*Present students, the most important thing is not to be dualistic.
Our original mind includes everything within itself.
It's always rich and sufficient within itself.
You should not lose your self-sufficient state of mind.
This does not mean a closed mind, but actually an empty mind and a ready mind.
If your mind is empty, it is always ready for anything.
It is open to everything.*
*In the beginner's mind, there are many possibilities.
In the expert's mind, there are few.
If you discriminate too much, you limit yourself.
If you're too demanding or too greedy, your mind will not be rich or self-sufficient.
If we lose our original self-sufficient mind, we will lose the precepts.

When your mind becomes demanding, when you long for something, when you end up violating your own precepts, not to tell a lie, not to steal, not to kill, not to be immoral and so forth, but if you keep your original mind, the precepts will keep themselves.*
*In the beginner's mind, there's no thought, "I have attained something."
All self-centered thoughts limit our vast mind.
When we have no thought of achievement, no thought of self, we are true beginners.
And we can really learn something.
The beginner's mind is the mind of compassion.
When our mind is compassionate, it is boundless.
Dogen Zenji, the founder of our school, always emphasized how important it is to resume our boundless original mind.
Then we are always true to ourselves in sympathy with all beings and can actually practice.*
*So, the most difficult thing is always to keep your beginner's mind.
There's no need of a deep understanding of Zen.
Even though you read much Zen literature, you must read each sentence with a fresh mind.
You should not say, "I know what Zen is," or "I've attained enlightenment."
This is also the real secret of the arts.
Always be a beginner.
Be very, very careful about this point.
If you start to practice Zazen, you will begin to appreciate your beginner's mind.*
It is the secret of Zen practice. [unclear: "Foucault Trudy"] chose this famous line in this: "In the beginner's mind, there are many possibilities.
In the expert's, there are few."
Reading this again and thinking about it, I take a little more seriously Suzuki Roshi's warning in there.
This is really difficult on the one hand, and also very natural on the other hand, if we practice, especially if we practice Zazen.
Because isn't it pretty hard to stay settled in openness, in trust, in receptivity, in this kind of feeling of beginner's mind?
We're just so primed by our conditioning to constrict around things.
To get tight, to get worried, to try to control and force things into a particular pattern.
And when we do that, always our self is right in the middle, whether we know it or not, at the moment.
We want it our way.
And we're pretty good at convincing ourselves that it's not that we want it our way.
It's just this is the way it should be.
It's the right way.
Don't you see?
I've become more and more familiar with this feeling of constriction.
I'm sure you study this too.
This kind of descent.
Maybe it's into expert's mind, I don't know.
But in my case, what I noticed is I get agitated, I get anxious.
I move a bit too fast, I jump in too quickly to do it the way I want to do it.
And lately what I've really tried to do is focus more and more on the feeling of release when it happens.
When it happens, back into something like beginner's mind, to really feel that deeply in mind and body, to experience that.
Not just to rush on like, "Oh, I'm glad I'm not upset anymore."
To feel the stomach soften, the eyes relax, whatever it is for you.
To feel the joy and ease.
That is also so natural to us.
And to not get so hooked by our Western fixation with, well, how do I fix this problem?
This problem of going back and forth like this?
Of course we want to apply various techniques.
We want to get good at pausing and taking a breath.
I want to get good at reminding myself about the Dharma, surround myself with support, see others as Buddha and my teachers.
And I think that's a good practice, which is all good for sure.
But it's not something that fixes anything.
And our fixed views and self-concepts easily overpower any number of great little practices and techniques, for sure.
So I really more and more think it's interesting to take refuge in noticing the good.
Noticing release.
Noticing and feeling and celebrating a little bit.
Noticing a little bit of happiness and openness.
And to take heart that I'm planting a wholesome seed by just noticing that.
Like noticing that my body and mind can do that.
Deeply reminding myself that that's possible.
That goes deep.
And that's also where the wonderful Yogacara Buddhist system comes in, with all the seeds in the warehouse that you can't see, but they're there.
They germinate and manifest, right?
But then in how you respond, you plant new seeds.
So it's a pay-it-forward system.
And how heartening that our little study of brain science seems to say the exact same thing.
Because the brain is so predictive and intensely involved in keeping you safe and organized at all times, you've often already blown past the warning signs and you're into trouble.
So the way forward in that system, just the same as Yogacara Buddhism, is to plant positive seeds for the future.
Notice, reinforce how you want to be.
So rather than something that we make happen, maybe our beginner's mind is something that we celebrate and notice and feel when it's present, when it's obvious to us.
Maybe in some deep way it's always present, but it's not always manifesting and showing itself, right?
But good news: it'll be back sooner or later.
It's our birthright and our nature.
And of course, we hope that over years or decades of practice, you notice in there he said maybe after one, two or three years of practice.
It was early days, there weren't people around him who practiced for 30 years.
So we hope after 10 or 20 or 30 years that more and more our default is these wholesome seeds germinating the openness of beginner's mind.
But to clarify one point here, beginner's mind doesn't mean that we are ignorant.
It doesn't mean we forget what we know.
If we have expertise in something, that's wonderful and valuable, right?
We should bring it forward.
We should use it for the good.
Bodhisattvas like Avalokiteshvara, with all of her different tools and implements, right?
We use our expertise to help beings and to make this a little better world.
You share and do good work with our expert knowledge.
And it's great when experts help us, it's fantastic.
I had a little experience of that today.
A couple of days ago I was trying to fix the ancient faucet in our old house.
It must be at least 50 years old.
I was trying to tighten it down because it was slipping, and I sheared off a bolt and the stub of the bolt got stuck inside the valve.
And I was so upset, I ruined the faucet.
And how am I going to get parts for this ancient faucet?
Why did [unclear: "India"] blah, blah, blah, blah, blah?
And it was wild.
This little mess-up affected me for quite a while.
Every time I went by the kitchen, I went, "Ah."
But then today there was a plumber here for something else, and I asked if he would look at my old faucet.
Firstly, he was really fascinated.
He crawled underneath and he took a little video of the plumbing and the kind of fixture it was, and he was playing it back and saying, "Wow, I've never seen this before."
And then he looked at my little issue and I explained what had happened.
And he said, "Oh," and he [unclear: "sat down his thumb"] and he was able to just, with his thumb, remove this little stub of a bolt.
It wasn't tight at all.
He handed it to me and said, "It's okay."
So I was so grateful for the expert mind that appeared before me.
So it's not about knowledge.
It's not about knowledge.
It's about attitude.
What attitude am I bringing right now?
Am I open?
Am I receptive?
Am I inclusive?
Am I using whatever knowledge is helpful here in a helpful way, supportive of the good?
Or is my attitude closed and fixed, excluding, righteous, my way or the highway?
Maybe righteousness is a better term than expert's mind, because we sure know what that is.
We don't always know when we're doing it because we're in the middle of it, but we can sure see it in others.
That's the other thing about these kinds of teachings, beginner's mind, expert's mind, righteousness, precepts, not precepts: it's no good to try to judge somebody else.
That's a violation.
That's expert mind.
That's a violation of the precepts right there.
We can only really work with our own mind and be as kind as we can to others.
So, a little scholastic side note and then a little story about this term.
Then I thought we'd have some conversations about it.
To really contemplate: how does expert's mind, beginner's mind, whether those terms are landing for you or some other terms, how does it show up for you?
Here's a scholastic note.
It turns out beginner's mind is not a clearly established Buddhist saying.
The two characters that are pronounced Shoshin in Sino-Japanese don't show up in most of the entire Buddhist canon.
They don't show up in the whole realm of literature called the Agamas.
This term doesn't show up in the early Buddhist teachings.
It does show up in the Prajnaparamita literature a fair bit, apparently.
So maybe it's a later innovation.
But the characters were not usually, and originally, translated as beginner's mind.
They were translated as initial aspiration.
Initial aspiration, which has a whole different feel to it, doesn't it?
And it's a positive.
We have to have a good initial aspiration when we take up practice or take up anything new.
But beginner's mind is so much more continuous than initial aspiration, right?
It's the aspiration of the beginning, the middle, and the end, and then back to the beginning again.
The beginner's mind includes more than just personal aspiration, but also includes everybody else.
It's our way of life for all beings.
It's our way-seeking mind.
So there's a little discussion going on about this recently in a priest list I'm on.
One of the people who commented was a direct student of Suzuki Roshi's, Shosan Vicki Austin, and she reported this memory.
She wrote in the email, "I'll bring in my experience of a day I was cleaning bookshelves in the room Suzuki Roshi used.
As I was cleaning, one of the books had some dust that would not come off.
So I picked it up and started dusting around the edges.
And the book fell open to a page that had clearly been very well used.
And what I saw brought tears to my eyes.
In the margin of the text was a long list of alternative translations of the same phrase.
Some erased more than once, some with insertions, some underlined once, and some underlined twice.
Suzuki Roshi had worked hard and taken a long time to choose a phrase that was easy to understand and practice with."
Isn't that a great story?
So maybe this is largely a Suzuki Roshi innovation, this term beginner's mind.
That's something else I want to share, but I think I'll save that for next week.
So we have a little more time.
Let's chant and turn off the recording, and then we'll have some discussion.
I think we'll use the breakout room.
So if that horrifies you, stick around anyway.
*May our intention equally extend to every being in place.
With the true merit of Buddha's way, beings are numberless, I vow to save them.
Divisions are inexhaustible, I vow to end them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable, I vow to* [unclear: "be comment"]*.*
